title: Anthropic says an unreleased Claude improved a Riemann zeta lower bound to 67.2%
subtitle: A research build of Claude, coordinating around 60 subagents over a day and a half, pushed a 37-year-old bound on zeros of the Riemann zeta function from 41.6% to 67.2%.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic disclosed this week that an unreleased research version of Claude produced a new lower bound for the proportion of non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function that lie on the critical line predicted by the Riemann hypothesis. The bound moved from 41.6% — a threshold that had stood as the best human result for about 37 years — to 67.2%. The work was checked by two Anthropic mathematicians and reviewed by outside experts Brian Conrey and Dan Goldston, and Anthropic published a formally verifiable proof alongside the paper.

This is not a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which remains one of mathematics' seven Millennium Prize problems. What Claude did was stitch together previously separate lines of work — treating a certain space of functions with both positive-definite and negative-definite parts together, rather than one at a time — and grind through the resulting search with roughly 60 coordinated subagents, 2,400 shell commands, and hundreds of Python scripts over about 36 hours. The value of the result is that it shows a language model can act as a working research collaborator on an open problem in analytic number theory, not that the underlying conjecture has been settled.

The disclosure lands in a wider argument about whether frontier models can meaningfully contribute to mathematics research rather than merely produce convincing-looking derivations. Earlier this year Anthropic put Claude on Fermat's Last Theorem in the Lean proof assistant, OpenAI's Astra took ten open math problems in July, and Cognition claimed a record RSA factorization with Devin this month. The Riemann zeta result is narrower than those headline swings but more clearly evaluable — a specific number, checked by named referees, with the proof available for anyone who wants to run it through a verifier.

For learners: the interesting skill here is not 'ask an LLM to solve a famous problem.' It is scoping. Claude did not attack the Riemann hypothesis directly — it pushed on an adjacent, well-defined bound where progress is measurable and existing techniques could be combined. If you are working on a hard problem with an AI collaborator, the biggest gain is usually not raw horsepower; it is finding a sub-problem where 'better' means a specific number moving in a specific direction, and where a human referee can check the answer without redoing the work.
